rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem: An electric dipole of length 2 cm is placed at an angle of \(30^\circ\) with an electric field \(2 \times 10^5\) N/C. If the dipole experiences a torque of \(8 \times 10^{-3}\) Nm, the magnitude of either charge of the dipole, is
rows.solution: The torque on a dipole in a uniform field is \(\tau = pE\sin\theta\), and the dipole moment of a dipole of length \(2a\) carrying charges \(\pm q\) is \(p = q(2a)\). So \(\tau = q(2a)E\sin\theta\). Substituting \(\tau = 8 \times 10^{-3}\) Nm, \(2a = 0.02\) m, \(E = 2 \times 10^5\) N/C and \(\theta = 30^\circ\) gives \(8 \times 10^{-3} = q \times 0.02 \times 2 \times 10^5 \times 0.5 = q \times 2000\). Hence \(q = 4 \times 10^{-6}\) C, so the magnitude of either charge is \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), matching the choice \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). Note that the 2 cm is the FULL length of the dipole, i.e. the separation of the two charges, not half of it.

rows.stem: Two long parallel wires kept 2 m apart carry 3A current each, in the same direction. The force per unit length on one wire due to the other is
rows.solution: [CBSE marking scheme: the Board declared this question defective. In place of a key the scheme prints "No option is correct. [Award one mark to each student]", so the mark was given to every candidate. The working below shows why.] For two long parallel wires a perpendicular distance \(d\) apart carrying currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), the force per unit length is \(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\), and it is ATTRACTIVE when the two currents flow in the same direction. Here \(I_1 = I_2 = 3\) A and \(d = 2\) m, so \(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{(2 \times 10^{-7})(3)(3)}{2} = 9 \times 10^{-7}\) N/m, and since the currents are in the same direction the wires attract each other. The correct entry would therefore read "\(9 \times 10^{-7}\) N/m, attractive". No printed option says that: the choice carrying the right magnitude \(9 \times 10^{-7}\) N/m calls the force repulsive, while the only choice that calls it attractive quotes \(9 \times 10^{-5}\) N/m, a hundred times too large. Hence no option is correct.

rows.stem: Which of the following has its permeability less than that of free space ?
rows.solution: A substance has permeability less than that of free space (\(\mu < \mu_0\), i.e. relative permeability \(\mu_r < 1\) and susceptibility \(\chi < 0\)) only if it is DIAMAGNETIC. A diamagnetic material has no net atomic magnetic moment; an applied field induces moments that oppose it, so the field inside is slightly weakened. Of the four substances listed, copper is diamagnetic. Aluminium is paramagnetic and nickel is ferromagnetic, so both have \(\mu > \mu_0\); copper chloride is paramagnetic, because the \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ion carries an unpaired electron and hence a permanent moment. So the substance is copper.

rows.stem: A square shaped coil of side 10 cm, having 100 turns is placed perpendicular to a magnetic field which is increasing at 1 T/s. The induced emf in the coil is
rows.solution: The coil is placed perpendicular to the field, so its plane is at right angles to \(\vec{B}\) and the flux through one turn is simply \(\phi = BA\), with \(A = (0.1\ \mathrm{m})^2 = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}\). By Faraday's law the magnitude of the emf induced in \(N\) turns is \(|\varepsilon| = N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NA\dfrac{dB}{dt}\), since only \(B\) is changing. Substituting \(N = 100\), \(A = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}\) and \(\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 1\) T/s gives \(|\varepsilon| = 100 \times 10^{-2} \times 1 = 1.0\) V, matching the choice 1.0 V.

rows.stem: Which one of the following electromagnetic radiation has the least wavelength ?
rows.solution: Going along the electromagnetic spectrum from long waves to short, the order is radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and finally gamma rays, with the wavelength decreasing and the photon energy \(E = hc/\lambda\) increasing all the way. Gamma rays, which come from nuclear transitions and radioactive decay, occupy the extreme short-wavelength end at below about \(10^{-12}\) m, shorter even than X-rays. Of the four radiations listed, microwaves are the longest and visible light is next, so the one with the least wavelength is gamma rays.

rows.stem:
In a Young's double-slit experiment, the screen is moved away from the plane of the slits. What will be its effect on the following ?
(i) Angular separation of the fringes.
(ii) Fringe-width.
rows.solution: The two quantities behave differently because only one of them depends on the screen distance \(D\). The angular separation of the fringes is \(\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}\), which involves only the wavelength and the slit separation, so moving the screen away does not change it and (i) remains constant. The fringe width actually measured on the screen is \(\beta = \dfrac{D\lambda}{d}\), which is directly proportional to \(D\), so moving the screen away makes the fringes wider and (ii) increases. The two are consistent with each other, since \(\beta = D\theta\): the same angular fan of fringes simply spreads over more of the screen. Hence the correct description is "(i) remains constant, but (ii) increases".

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The energy of a photon of wavelength \(\lambda\) is
rows.solution:
A photon of frequency \(
u\) carries energy \(E = h
u\), where \(h\) is Planck's constant. For an electromagnetic wave in vacuum the frequency and wavelength are related by \(c = 
u\lambda\), so \(
u = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\). Substituting gives \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\), so the photon energy is inversely proportional to the wavelength. A dimensional check confirms it: \(hc\) has units of energy \(	imes\) length, and dividing by a length leaves an energy. So the energy of the photon is \(hc/\lambda\).

rows.stem: The ratio of the nuclear densities of two nuclei having mass numbers 64 and 125 is
rows.solution: The radius of a nucleus of mass number \(A\) is \(R = R_0 A^{1/3}\) with \(R_0 \approx 1.2\) fm, so its volume is \(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A\), which is directly proportional to \(A\). Its mass is also very nearly proportional to \(A\), being about \(A m_N\) where \(m_N\) is the mass of a nucleon. Hence the nuclear density is \(\rho = \dfrac{A m_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3 m_N}{4\pi R_0^3}\), in which \(A\) has cancelled completely. Nuclear density is therefore the same for every nucleus, about \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), and the required ratio is 1.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: During the formation of a p-n junction :

options.label: C
options.text: both the diffusion current and drift current remain constant.

options.label: D
options.text: diffusion current remains almost constant but drift current increases till both currents become equal.

rows.solution: As soon as the p- and n-regions are joined, the large concentration gradient across the junction makes holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side; this constitutes the DIFFUSION current. The carriers that leave uncover immobile ionised acceptors on the p-side and donors on the n-side, forming the depletion region, and these fixed charges set up an electric field directed from n to p. That field sweeps any minority carrier which strays into the depletion region across to the other side, giving the DRIFT current, which is in the opposite sense to the diffusion current. As diffusion continues the depletion region widens, the field grows stronger and so the drift current grows, while the diffusion current stays almost unchanged. The junction reaches equilibrium when the two become equal, so that the net current is zero and a steady barrier potential exists. So during the formation of the junction, the diffusion current remains almost constant but the drift current increases till both currents become equal.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The diagram shows four energy level of an electron in Bohr model of hydrogen atom. Identify the transition in which the emitted photon will have the highest energy.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the four options are the bare labels I, II, III and IV, which exist ONLY in the drawing, so the figure is the entire question. Described here: an energy-level diagram of four horizontal levels labelled at the right n = 4, n = 3, n = 2 and n = 1 from top to bottom, crossed by four downward arrows each labelled with a Roman numeral I, II, III or IV. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: which pair of levels each numbered arrow connects — that mapping is precisely what decides the largest energy drop and therefore the answer. Page idx 6.
rows.solution: For hydrogen the Bohr energy levels are \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\) eV, giving \(E_1 = -13.6\) eV, \(E_2 = -3.4\) eV, \(E_3 = -1.51\) eV and \(E_4 = -0.85\) eV. The photon emitted in a downward transition carries energy equal to the difference between the two levels, so the most energetic photon comes from the transition with the largest energy drop. Reading the four arrows off the diagram: transition I runs from \(n = 3\) to \(n = 1\), giving \(13.6 - 1.51 = 12.09\) eV; transition II runs from \(n = 4\) to \(n = 3\), giving \(1.51 - 0.85 = 0.66\) eV; transition III runs from \(n = 2\) to \(n = 1\), giving \(13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2\) eV; and transition IV runs from \(n = 3\) to \(n = 2\), giving \(3.4 - 1.51 = 1.89\) eV. The useful point is that the levels crowd closer together as \(n\) increases, so a long-looking arrow between high levels can carry far less energy than a shorter one ending on \(n = 1\). The largest of the four is 12.09 eV, so the highest-energy photon is emitted in transition I.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: Which of the following graphs correctly represents the variation of a particle momentum with its associated de-Broglie wavelength ?

options.label: A
options.text: a plot of \(p\) (vertical axis) against \(\lambda\) (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a straight line of constant positive slope, rising to the right and not passing through the origin

options.label: B
options.text: a plot of \(p\) (vertical axis) against \(\lambda\) (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a curve rising to the right, gently at first and then more and more steeply (concave upwards)

options.label: C
options.text: a plot of \(p\) (vertical axis) against \(\lambda\) (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a straight line of constant negative slope, starting high on the \(p\)-axis and falling steadily to the right

options.label: D
options.text: a plot of \(p\) (vertical axis) against \(\lambda\) (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a curve falling steeply from near the \(p\)-axis and then flattening towards the \(\lambda\)-axis (a rectangular-hyperbola shape)

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all four options are DRAWN GRAPHS with no text of their own; only the axis labels p and \(\lambda\) are printed. Each option's axes and curve shape are described in its option text above, which preserves the discrimination the question tests (the student must still know p = h/\(\lambda\)) rather than naming a winner. Page idx 6.
rows.solution: The de Broglie relation is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\), which rearranges to \(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\), i.e. \(p\lambda = h = \) constant. Momentum is therefore INVERSELY proportional to the de Broglie wavelength, and a graph of \(p\) against \(\lambda\) is a rectangular hyperbola: it falls steeply near the \(p\)-axis and then flattens out, approaching the \(\lambda\)-axis asymptotically without ever touching either axis. The two straight-line graphs must be wrong because they describe a linear relation between \(p\) and \(\lambda\), and the curve that rises ever more steeply is wrong because it has \(p\) increasing with \(\lambda\), the opposite of the required behaviour. So the correct graph is the one with the rectangular-hyperbola shape, falling steeply and then flattening towards the \(\lambda\)-axis.

rows.stem: The capacitors, each of 4 \(\mu\mathrm{F}\) are to be connected in such a way that the effective capacitance of the combination is 6 \(\mu\mathrm{F}\). This can be achieved by connecting

options.label: C
options.text: Two of them connected in series and the combination in parallel to the third.

options.label: D
options.text: Two of them connected in parallel and the combination in series to the third.

rows.solution: Let the three capacitors be \(C_1 = C_2 = C_3 = 4\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and test the arrangements. Two in series give \(\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \dfrac{4 \times 4}{8} = 2\ \mu\mathrm{F}\); putting that combination in parallel with the third simply adds, \(2 + 4 = 6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), which is exactly what is wanted. The other arrangements miss: all three in parallel give \(4 + 4 + 4 = 12\ \mu\mathrm{F}\); all three in series give \(\dfrac{4}{3}\ \mu\mathrm{F}\); and two in parallel (\(8\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)) placed in series with the third give \(\dfrac{8 \times 4}{12} = \dfrac{8}{3}\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). So the required connection is two of them connected in series and the combination in parallel to the third.

rows.stem: Which of the following statements about a series LCR circuit connected to an ac source is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: If the frequency of the source is increased, the impedance of the circuit first decreases and then increases.

options.label: B
options.text: If the net reactance \((X_L - X_C)\) of circuit becomes equal to its resistance, then the current leads the voltage by \(45^\circ\).

options.label: C
options.text: At resonance, the voltage drop across the inductor is more than that across the capacitor.

options.label: D
options.text: At resonance, the voltage drop across the capacitor is more than that across the inductor.

rows.solution: For a series LCR circuit the impedance is \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}\) with \(X_L = \omega L\) and \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\). At low frequency \(X_C\) is very large, at high frequency \(X_L\) is very large, and at the resonant frequency \(X_L = X_C\) so that \(Z = R\), its least possible value. Raising the frequency from a low value therefore makes the impedance first DECREASE to \(R\) and then INCREASE again, which is the first statement. The others fail. If the net reactance \((X_L - X_C)\) equals \(R\) then \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R} = 1\), so the phase angle is \(45^\circ\); but a positive net reactance means the circuit is inductive, so the current LAGS the voltage rather than leading it. And at resonance the voltage drops across the inductor and the capacitor are equal in magnitude and exactly opposite in phase, so neither exceeds the other. Hence the correct statement is that increasing the source frequency makes the impedance first decrease and then increase.

rows.stem: According to Huygens principle, the amplitude of secondary wavelets is

options.label: A
options.text: equal in both the forward and the backward directions.

options.label: B
options.text: maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction.

options.label: C
options.text: large in the forward direction and small in the backward direction.

options.label: D
options.text: small in the forward direction and large in the backward direction.

rows.solution: In Huygens' construction every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets, and the new wavefront is their forward envelope. The wavelets are not, however, emitted equally in all directions: their amplitude carries an obliquity or inclination factor proportional to \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \cos\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is measured from the forward direction of propagation. This factor equals 1 straight ahead (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)) and falls to zero straight back (\(\theta = 180^\circ\)). The factor is needed precisely because a construction without it would also predict a backward-travelling wave, which is never observed. So the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The radius of the n\(^{\text{th}}\) orbit in Bohr model of hydrogen atom is proportional to
rows.solution: In the Bohr model the electrostatic attraction of the nucleus supplies the centripetal force, \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), and the angular momentum is quantised, \(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\). From the second relation \(v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r}\); substituting this into the first and simplifying gives \(r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m e^2}\). Every factor except \(n^2\) is a constant, so the radius of the \(n\)th orbit is proportional to \(n^2\). (For hydrogen this gives the Bohr radius \(r_1 = 0.53\) angstrom, with the second orbit four times and the third nine times as large.) So the radius is proportional to \(n^2\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The resistance of an intrinsic semiconductor decreases with increase in its temperature.

**Reason (R) :** The number of conduction electrons as well as hole increase in an intrinsic semiconductor with rise in its temperature.
rows.context:
In question number 16 to 18 two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :
(A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
(B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(C) Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.
(D) Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution: Raising the temperature of an intrinsic semiconductor gives more valence electrons enough thermal energy to cross the forbidden energy gap into the conduction band. Every electron that makes the jump leaves a hole behind, so the number densities of conduction electrons and of holes rise together and remain equal, \(n_e = n_h = n_i\). The conductivity is \(\sigma = e(n_e\mu_e + n_h\mu_h)\); the extra lattice vibrations at higher temperature do reduce the mobilities slightly, but the increase in carrier number is far larger, so the conductivity rises and the resistance falls. The Assertion is therefore true, the Reason is also true, and the multiplication of charge carriers described in the Reason is exactly the mechanism that produces the fall in resistance. So both statements are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

**Reason (R) :** All the resistors are connected in parallel

In question number 16 to 18 two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :
(A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
(B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(C) Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.
(D) Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the assertion refers to 'the given network' and the reason makes a claim about how that network is wired, so the drawing carries the whole question. Described here: a resistor network drawn between a terminal marked A on the left and a terminal marked B on the right, containing FIVE resistors, every one of them labelled 2R. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the topology — which resistors sit in which branch and which nodes they join — since that is exactly what decides both whether the equivalent resistance is 2R and whether the resistors are all in parallel. Page idx 10.
rows.solution: Name the four junctions along the horizontal line \(A\), \(M\), \(N\), \(B\) in order. The five resistors, each of value \(2R\), then connect \(A\)-\(M\), \(M\)-\(N\) and \(N\)-\(B\) along that line, \(A\)-\(N\) along the upper branch, and \(M\)-\(B\) along the lower branch. This is a Wheatstone bridge with \(M\)-\(N\) as the bridge arm, and it is BALANCED, because the ratio of the resistances in the two arms is the same on both sides, \(\dfrac{2R}{2R} = \dfrac{2R}{2R}\). Junctions \(M\) and \(N\) are therefore at the same potential, no current passes through the \(M\)-\(N\) resistor, and it may be removed without altering anything. What remains is two paths from \(A\) to \(B\), namely \(A \rightarrow M \rightarrow B\) and \(A \rightarrow N \rightarrow B\), each of two resistors in series, i.e. \(2R + 2R = 4R\), and these two are in parallel, giving \(\dfrac{4R}{2} = 2R\). The equivalent resistance between \(A\) and \(B\) really is \(2R\), so the Assertion is TRUE. The Reason, however, is FALSE: the resistors are clearly not all in parallel, since each path carries two of them one after the other in series; five \(2R\) resistors genuinely in parallel would give only \(\dfrac{2R}{5}\). So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The deflecting torque acting on a current carrying loop is zero when its plane is perpendicular to the direction of magnetic field.

**Reason (R) :** The deflecting torque acting on a loop of magnetic moment \(\vec{m}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by the dot product of \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\).
rows.context:
In question number 16 to 18 two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :
(A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
(B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(C) Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.
(D) Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution: The deflecting torque on a current-carrying loop of magnetic moment \(\vec{m}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is the CROSS product \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}\), of magnitude \(mB\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\). The magnetic moment points along the normal to the plane of the loop, so if the PLANE of the loop is perpendicular to the field, the normal, and hence \(\vec{m}\), is PARALLEL to the field; then \(\theta = 0\), \(\sin\theta = 0\) and the torque vanishes. The Assertion is therefore true. The Reason states the torque as the dot product of \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\), and that is false on two counts: torque is a vector while a dot product is a scalar, and it is \(-\vec{m}\cdot\vec{B}\) that gives the potential energy of the loop, not its torque. (Notice also that the dot product would be a MAXIMUM in the very configuration where the torque is zero, so the Reason even predicts the opposite of the Assertion.) So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem: Draw a graph showing the variation of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Indicate the region in which the nuclear force is (a) attractive and (b) repulsive.
rows.solution: Plot the potential energy \(U\) of a pair of nucleons on the vertical axis against their separation \(r\) on the horizontal axis. The curve begins high and POSITIVE at very small separations, falls steeply, crosses the \(r\)-axis at about 0.8 fm, dips to a minimum of roughly \(-100\) MeV at a separation \(r_0 \approx 0.8\) fm, and then climbs back, approaching zero asymptotically once \(r\) exceeds a few femtometres. Since the force is the negative gradient of the potential energy, \(F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr}\), the slope of the curve fixes the nature of the force on each side of the minimum. (a) ATTRACTIVE region: for \(r > r_0\) the curve RISES with increasing \(r\), so \(\dfrac{dU}{dr} > 0\) and the force is negative, i.e. directed so as to pull the nucleons together. This is the ordinary attractive nuclear force that binds the nucleus, and it dies away rapidly beyond a few femtometres, showing that the nuclear force is short-ranged. (b) REPULSIVE region: for \(r < r_0\) the curve FALLS steeply with increasing \(r\), so \(\dfrac{dU}{dr} < 0\) and the force is positive, i.e. it pushes the nucleons apart. This strong short-range repulsive core is what prevents nucleons from collapsing into one another and keeps nuclear matter at an almost constant density. At \(r = r_0\) itself the potential energy is a minimum and the net force is zero, which is the equilibrium separation of the pair.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: How will the De Broglie wavelength associated with an electron be affected when the (i) velocity of the electron decreases ? and (ii) accelerating potential is increased ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution: (i) EFFECT OF DECREASING THE VELOCITY. The de Broglie wavelength associated with a particle of momentum \(p\) is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\), and for an electron of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) this is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}\). The wavelength is therefore inversely proportional to the speed. If the velocity of the electron DECREASES, its momentum decreases and the de Broglie wavelength INCREASES. (ii) EFFECT OF INCREASING THE ACCELERATING POTENTIAL. An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference \(V\) acquires kinetic energy \(eV\), so \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV\) and its momentum is \(p = mv = \sqrt{2meV}\). Hence \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\), that is \(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\). If the accelerating potential is INCREASED the electron emerges faster and more energetic, so the de Broglie wavelength DECREASES, falling as the inverse square root of the potential. (Numerically \(\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\) nm with \(V\) in volts.)

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem: How would the stopping potential for a given photosensitive surface change if (i) the frequency of the incident radiation were increased ? and (ii) the intensity of incident radiation were decreased ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution: By Einstein's photoelectric equation the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is \(K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0\), where \(\phi_0\) is the work function of the surface. The stopping potential \(V_0\) is the retarding potential that just stops the fastest electrons, so \(eV_0 = K_{\max}\) and therefore \(V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\). (i) EFFECT OF INCREASING THE FREQUENCY. For a GIVEN photosensitive surface \(\phi_0\) is fixed, so \(V_0\) is a straight-line function of the frequency with the positive slope \(\dfrac{h}{e}\). Increasing the frequency of the incident radiation therefore INCREASES the stopping potential, because each photon delivers more energy and the ejected electrons emerge with greater maximum kinetic energy. (ii) EFFECT OF DECREASING THE INTENSITY. The intensity fixes how many photons arrive per second, not how much energy each one carries. Reducing the intensity reduces the number of photoelectrons and hence the saturation photocurrent, but it leaves \(K_{\max}\) untouched. The stopping potential therefore REMAINS THE SAME.

rows.stem:
Identify the electromagnetic wave whose wavelengths range is from about
(a) \(10^{-12}\) m to about \(10^{-8}\) m.
(b) \(10^{-3}\) m to about \(10^{-1}\) m.
Write one use of each.
rows.solution: (a) Wavelengths from about \(10^{-12}\) m to about \(10^{-8}\) m are X-RAYS. They are produced when fast electrons are suddenly stopped by a metal target of high atomic number. One use: as a diagnostic tool in medicine, for imaging bones and detecting fractures. (Other acceptable uses are the treatment of certain cancers and the study of crystal structure by diffraction. Since \(10^{-12}\) m lies right where the X-ray and gamma-ray bands overlap, the marking scheme also accepts gamma rays here, with the destruction of cancer cells as a use.) (b) Wavelengths from about \(10^{-3}\) m to about \(10^{-1}\) m are MICROWAVES. They are produced by special vacuum tubes such as klystrons, magnetrons and Gunn diodes. One use: in radar systems for aircraft navigation, their short wavelength allowing them to travel in narrow, well-directed beams. (Microwave ovens, which heat food by resonantly exciting water molecules, are an equally acceptable use.)

rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem:
Depict the orientation of an electric dipole in (a) stable and (b) unstable equilibrium in an external uniform electric field.
Write the potential energy of the dipole in each case.
rows.solution: The potential energy of a dipole of moment \(\vec{p}\) in a uniform field \(\vec{E}\) is \(U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta\), and the torque on it is \(\tau = pE\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{E}\). Equilibrium requires zero torque, so \(\sin\theta = 0\) and only \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ\) are possible; the potential energy decides which of the two is stable. (a) STABLE EQUILIBRIUM. Draw the uniform field as a set of parallel arrows pointing (say) to the right, and draw the dipole ALONG them, with \(\vec{p}\) pointing the same way as \(\vec{E}\), so that \(\theta = 0^\circ\). The potential energy is then \(U = -pE\), the MINIMUM value it can take, and any small angular displacement produces a restoring torque that brings the dipole back. (b) UNSTABLE EQUILIBRIUM. Draw the same field arrows but turn the dipole round, so that \(\vec{p}\) points OPPOSITE to \(\vec{E}\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ\). The potential energy is then \(U = +pE\), the MAXIMUM value, and the least disturbance produces a torque that turns the dipole still further away, until it flips into the stable position.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: Write the expression for the Lorentz force on a particle of charge q moving with a velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). When is the magnitude of this force maximum ? Show that no work is done by this force on the particle during its motion from a point \(\vec{r}_1\) to point \(\vec{r}_2\).
rows.solution: EXPRESSION FOR THE LORENTZ FORCE. A charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) experiences the magnetic (Lorentz) force \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\), whose magnitude is \(F = qvB\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\). WHEN IS IT MAXIMUM. Since \(q\), \(v\) and \(B\) are fixed, \(F\) is greatest when \(\sin\theta\) is greatest, i.e. when \(\theta = 90^\circ\). So the magnitude of the force is MAXIMUM when the velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field, and then \(F_{\max} = qvB\). (It is zero when the particle moves parallel or antiparallel to the field.) NO WORK IS DONE. Being a cross product, \(\vec{F}\) is by construction perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\). The work done in a small displacement \(d\vec{r} = \vec{v}\,dt\) is therefore \(dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}\,dt = 0\) at every instant, and integrating along the path from \(\vec{r}_1\) to \(\vec{r}_2\) gives \(W = \int_{\vec{r}_1}^{\vec{r}_2}\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0\). Equivalently, since the angle between the force and the displacement is always \(90^\circ\), \(W = F\,|\vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1|\cos 90^\circ = 0\). The magnetic force can therefore change the DIRECTION of the particle's velocity but never its speed or its kinetic energy, which is why a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle at constant speed.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A long straight wire AB carries a current I. A particle (mass m and charge q) moves with a velocity \(\vec{v}\), parallel to the wire, at a distance d from it as shown in the figure. Obtain the expression for the force experienced by the particle and mention its directions.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the question asks for the DIRECTION of the force, and the geometry that fixes it is printed only in the drawing. Described here: a long straight vertical wire whose lower end is labelled A and upper end B, carrying a current labelled I; to the right of it a dot labelled 'Particle', joined to the wire by a horizontal double-headed dimension line labelled d; a short arrow at the particle is labelled \(\vec{v}\). DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the SENSE of the current arrow on the wire and the sense of the velocity arrow at the particle — the stem says only that \(\vec{v}\) is parallel to the wire, so whether it runs with or against I is carried by the figure alone and is what decides the direction asked for. Page idx 12.
rows.solution: Read the geometry off the figure first: the wire is vertical with A at the bottom and B at the top, and the current \(I\) flows UPWARD from A to B; the particle lies a perpendicular distance \(d\) to the RIGHT of the wire, and its velocity \(\vec{v}\) points DOWNWARD, that is, antiparallel to the current. MAGNITUDE. The magnetic field of a long straight wire at a perpendicular distance \(d\) is \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\), and by the right-hand thumb rule it is directed INTO the plane of the paper at the particle's position. The velocity lies in the plane of the paper, so \(\vec{v}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\) and \(\sin\theta = 1\). Hence the force experienced by the particle is \(F = qvB\sin 90^\circ = qvB = \dfrac{\mu_0 q v I}{2\pi d}\). DIRECTION. Applying \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\) with \(\vec{v}\) pointing down the page and \(\vec{B}\) into the page, the cross product points to the RIGHT, so for a positive charge the force is directed horizontally AWAY from the wire: the interaction is repulsive. This is exactly what should be expected, because a positive charge drifting downwards is equivalent to a small current element directed downwards, i.e. ANTIPARALLEL to \(I\), and antiparallel currents repel one another. (Had the figure shown \(\vec{v}\) parallel to \(I\) instead, the same reasoning would give a force towards the wire; and for a negative charge each conclusion reverses.) Note also that this force, being perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\), does no work on the particle.

rows.stem: The potential difference applied across a given conductor is doubled. How will this affect (i) the mobility of electrons and (ii) the current density in the conductor ? Justify your answers.
rows.solution: (i) EFFECT ON THE MOBILITY OF ELECTRONS: NO EFFECT. Mobility is defined as the drift speed acquired per unit applied electric field, \(\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E}\). Since the drift speed itself is \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\), this gives \(\mu = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}\), which contains only the electronic charge, the electronic mass and the relaxation time. The relaxation time is a property of the conductor at a given temperature, so nothing in the expression depends on the applied potential difference. Doubling \(V\) doubles the field and doubles the drift velocity, but their RATIO is unchanged, so the mobility is unaffected. (Equivalently, \(\mu = \dfrac{v_d l}{V} = \dfrac{l}{enAR}\), again independent of \(V\).) (ii) EFFECT ON THE CURRENT DENSITY: IT DOUBLES. The current density is \(J = \dfrac{I}{A}\), and by Ohm's law \(I = \dfrac{V}{R}\), so \(J = \dfrac{V}{RA}\). For a GIVEN conductor at constant temperature both \(R\) and \(A\) are fixed, so \(J \propto V\) and doubling the potential difference doubles the current density. The same conclusion follows from \(J = \sigma E\): doubling \(V\) doubles \(E\) while the conductivity \(\sigma\) stays the same.

rows.stem:
Two coils \(\mathrm{C}_1\) and \(\mathrm{C}_2\) are placed close to each other. The magnetic flux \(\phi_2\) linked with the coil \(\mathrm{C}_2\) varies with the current \(\mathrm{I}_1\) flowing in coil \(\mathrm{C}_1\), as shown in the figure. Find
(i) the mutual inductance of the arrangement, and
(ii) the rate of change of current \(\left(\dfrac{d\mathrm{I}_1}{dt}\right)\) that will induce an emf of 100 V in coil \(\mathrm{C}_2\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (i) asks for the mutual inductance, which on this question is the GRADIENT of the printed graph and appears nowhere in the stem. Described here: a graph whose vertical axis is labelled \(\phi_2\) (wb) and whose horizontal axis is labelled \(\mathrm{I}_1\) (A), both arrowed, with the origin marked 0; the plot is a single straight line rising from the origin. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the tick values marked on the two axes, and hence the gradient — those numbers ARE the answer to part (i) and carry through to part (ii). Page idx 14.
rows.solution: (i) MUTUAL INDUCTANCE. The flux linked with the second coil is proportional to the current in the first, \(\phi_2 = M I_1\), where \(M\) is the mutual inductance of the arrangement. Comparing this with the equation of a straight line through the origin shows that \(M\) is simply the SLOPE of the given graph. Reading the graph, the line passes through the origin and through the point \(I_1 = 6\) A, \(\phi_2 = 15\) Wb, so \(M = \dfrac{\phi_2}{I_1} = \dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5\) H. (Any other point on the line gives the same value, as it must for a straight line through the origin.) (ii) RATE OF CHANGE OF CURRENT. The emf induced in \(\mathrm{C}_2\) by a changing current in \(\mathrm{C}_1\) is \(|\varepsilon_2| = M\dfrac{d\mathrm{I}_1}{dt}\). Setting \(|\varepsilon_2| = 100\) V and using \(M = 2.5\) H, \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{I}_1}{dt} = \dfrac{|\varepsilon_2|}{M} = \dfrac{100}{2.5} = 40\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}\). So the current in the first coil must change at 40 amperes per second.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem:
A plane wave-front propagating in a medium of refractive index '\(\mu_1\)' is incident on a plane surface making an angle of incidence (i). It enters into a medium of refractive index \(\mu_2\) \((\mu_2 > \mu_1)\).

Use Huygen's construction of secondary wavelets to trace the retracted wave-front. Hence verify Snell's law of refraction.
rows.solution: CONSTRUCTION. Let \(PP'\) be the plane surface separating medium 1 (refractive index \(\mu_1\), wave speed \(v_1\)) from medium 2 (refractive index \(\mu_2\), wave speed \(v_2\)). Let the plane wavefront \(AB\) be incident on it at an angle \(i\), with \(A\) on the surface and \(B\) the point where the wavefront meets the ray that will strike the surface at \(C\). Let \(\tau\) be the time the wavefront takes to travel from \(B\) to \(C\), so that \(BC = v_1\tau\). By Huygens' principle, the instant the wavefront reaches \(A\) a secondary wavelet sets out from \(A\) into the second medium. In the same time \(\tau\) it grows into a sphere of radius \(AE = v_2\tau\). Draw the tangent plane \(CE\) from \(C\) to this sphere: \(CE\) is the REFRACTED WAVEFRONT, and the refracted rays are perpendicular to it. VERIFICATION OF SNELL'S LAW. Because \(CE\) is a tangent, \(AE \perp CE\); and because \(AB\) is a wavefront, \(BC \perp AB\). So \(ABC\) and \(AEC\) are right-angled triangles sharing the hypotenuse \(AC\). The angle of incidence and the angle of refraction appear in them as \(\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1\tau}{AC}\) and \(\sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2\tau}{AC}\). Dividing one by the other, the common factors \(\tau\) and \(AC\) cancel and \(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\). Since the refractive index of a medium is \(\mu = \dfrac{c}{v}\), we have \(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\), and therefore \(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\), that is \(\mu_1\sin i = \mu_2\sin r\). This is Snell's law of refraction. Here \(\mu_2 > \mu_1\), so \(v_2 < v_1\), hence \(\sin r < \sin i\) and the refracted wavefront bends TOWARDS the normal, as it should on entering a denser medium.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: Using Huygen's construction, show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection.
rows.solution: [CBSE marking scheme: the printed proof states the congruence as "triangle AEC is congruent to triangle AEC" -- a triangle compared with itself, which establishes nothing. The two triangles being compared are \(AEC\) and \(CBA\), and the three facts the scheme lists immediately above that line are exactly what proves them congruent; its conclusion \(\angle i = \angle r\) is correct.] CONSTRUCTION. Let \(MN\) be the reflecting surface and let the plane wavefront \(AB\) be incident on it at an angle \(i\), with \(A\) on the surface and \(B\) the point where the wavefront meets the ray that strikes the surface at \(C\). If \(v\) is the speed of the wave in the medium and \(\tau\) is the time the wavefront takes to advance from \(B\) to \(C\), then \(BC = v\tau\). By Huygens' principle a secondary wavelet starts out from \(A\) the moment the wavefront arrives there, and in the same time \(\tau\) it becomes a hemisphere of radius \(AE = v\tau\) in the same medium. Draw the tangent plane \(CE\) from \(C\) to this sphere: \(CE\) is the REFLECTED WAVEFRONT. VERIFICATION OF THE LAW OF REFLECTION. Compare the right-angled triangles \(AEC\) and \(CBA\). First, \(AE = CB = v\tau\), since both were traced out in the same time at the same speed. Second, \(\angle AEC = \angle CBA = 90^\circ\), because the tangent \(CE\) is perpendicular to the radius \(AE\), and \(BC\) is perpendicular to the wavefront \(AB\). Third, \(AC\) is common to both and is the hypotenuse of each. By the RHS criterion the two triangles are congruent, so their corresponding angles are equal: \(\angle BAC = \angle ECA\). But \(\angle BAC\) is the angle of incidence \(i\) and \(\angle ECA\) is the angle of reflection \(r\) -- the angle a wavefront makes with the surface equals the angle the corresponding ray makes with the normal. Hence \(\angle i = \angle r\): the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Since the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the plane of the diagram, the law of reflection is verified in full.

rows.stem:
An alternating voltage of 220 V is applied across a device X. A current of 0.22 A flows in the circuit and it lags behind the applied voltage in phase by \(\pi/2\) radian. When the same voltage is applied across another device Y, the current in the circuit remains the same and it is in phase with the applied voltage.
(i) Name the devices X and Y and,
(ii) Calculate the current flowing in the circuit when the same voltage is applied across the series combination of X and Y.
rows.solution: (i) IDENTIFYING THE DEVICES. Across device X the current LAGS the applied voltage by \(\pi/2\) radian, that is by a quarter of a cycle. A pure inductor is the circuit element in which the current lags the voltage by exactly \(90^\circ\), so X is an INDUCTOR. Across device Y the current is IN PHASE with the applied voltage, which is the behaviour of a pure resistor, so Y is a RESISTOR. (ii) CURRENT IN THE SERIES COMBINATION. The same 220 V drives the same 0.22 A through each device separately, so \(X_L = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{220}{0.22} = 1000\ \Omega\) and \(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{220}{0.22} = 1000\ \Omega\). When X and Y are joined in SERIES the resistance and the reactance do not add arithmetically; they add in quadrature, giving the impedance \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{(1000)^2 + (1000)^2} = 1000\sqrt{2}\ \Omega\). The current is therefore \(I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{220}{1000\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{0.22}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.11\sqrt{2}\), so \(I_{rms} \approx 0.16\) A. (The result is larger than half of 0.22 A precisely because of the quadrature addition; the phase angle of the combination is \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{X_L}{R} = 45^\circ\).)

rows.stem: State the basic principle behind the working of an ac generator. Briefly describe its working and obtain the expression for the instantaneous value of emf induced.
rows.solution: PRINCIPLE. An ac generator works on the principle of ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION: whenever the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an emf is induced in it. CONSTRUCTION AND WORKING. A rectangular coil, the armature, of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) is mounted on an axle in a uniform magnetic field \(B\), with the axis of rotation perpendicular to the field. An external agent rotates the coil steadily with angular speed \(\omega\). As it turns, the angle between the normal to the coil and the field changes continuously, so the flux threading the coil changes continuously and an emf is induced in it. The two ends of the coil are joined to two SLIP RINGS, against which carbon brushes press to carry the current out to the external circuit. Because each end of the coil stays permanently connected to the same ring, the emf delivered to the circuit reverses in sign every half revolution, so the output is ALTERNATING. EXPRESSION FOR THE INSTANTANEOUS EMF. Let the normal to the coil make an angle \(\theta = \omega t\) with \(\vec{B}\), measuring time from the instant the coil's plane is perpendicular to the field. The flux linked with one turn at time \(t\) is then \(\phi_B = BA\cos\omega t\). By Faraday's law, for \(N\) turns, \(\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi_B}{dt} = -NBA\dfrac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t)\). Differentiating, \(\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t\). This is the required instantaneous emf. It is sinusoidal with peak value \(\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega\), so it may be written \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t\); the emf is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field (the flux is then changing fastest) and zero when the plane is perpendicular to it.

rows.stem:
(a) Briefly describe how the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased.
(b) A galvanometer shows full scale deflection for current \(\mathrm{I}_g\). A resistance \(\mathrm{R}_1\) is required to convert it into a voltmeter of range \((0 - \mathrm{V})\) and a resistance \(\mathrm{R}_2\) to convert it into a voltmeter of range \((0 - 2\mathrm{V})\). Find the resistance of the galvanometer.
rows.solution: (a) INCREASING THE CURRENT SENSITIVITY. The current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is the deflection produced per unit current, \(\dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{NBA}{k}\), where \(N\) is the number of turns of the coil, \(B\) the radial magnetic field, \(A\) the area of the coil and \(k\) the torsional constant of the suspension. It can therefore be increased by any of the following: increasing the number of turns \(N\) in the coil; increasing the magnetic field \(B\), by using stronger permanent magnets together with a soft-iron cylindrical core; increasing the area \(A\) of the coil; or decreasing the torsional constant \(k\), by using a suspension such as a thin phosphor-bronze strip, which twists easily. (b) RESISTANCE OF THE GALVANOMETER. A galvanometer of resistance \(G\) is converted into a voltmeter by placing a high resistance \(R\) in SERIES with it, chosen so that the full-scale current \(I_g\) flows when the full range voltage is applied across the combination: \(V = I_g(R + G)\), i.e. \(R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G\). For the range \((0 - \mathrm{V})\): \(\mathrm{R}_1 = \dfrac{V}{\mathrm{I}_g} - G\) ... (1). For the range \((0 - 2\mathrm{V})\): \(\mathrm{R}_2 = \dfrac{2V}{\mathrm{I}_g} - G\) ... (2). From (1), \(\dfrac{V}{\mathrm{I}_g} = \mathrm{R}_1 + G\). Substituting this into (2) gives \(\mathrm{R}_2 = 2(\mathrm{R}_1 + G) - G = 2\mathrm{R}_1 + G\). Hence the resistance of the galvanometer is \(G = \mathrm{R}_2 - 2\mathrm{R}_1\).

rows.stem:
(i) Differentiate between 'distance of closest approach' and 'impact parameter'.
(ii) Determine the distance of closest approach when an alpha particle of kinetic energy 3.95 MeV approaches a nucleus of Z = 79, stops and reverses its directions.
rows.solution: (i) THE DISTINCTION. The DISTANCE OF CLOSEST APPROACH is the least separation that an alpha particle reaches from the CENTRE of the nucleus in a head-on collision. At that point the particle has momentarily come to rest, so the whole of its initial kinetic energy has been converted into electrostatic potential energy. It is measured along the line of approach, it depends on the ENERGY of the alpha particle (the faster the particle the closer it gets), and it gives an upper limit on the size of the nucleus. The IMPACT PARAMETER is the perpendicular distance of the INITIAL velocity vector of the alpha particle from the centre of the nucleus, i.e. the perpendicular distance between the nucleus and the line along which the particle would have travelled had there been no force. It is a measure of how well the particle is aimed rather than of its energy, and it decides the angle of scattering: a small impact parameter gives large-angle scattering, a large one gives only a small deflection. Only a head-on collision, for which the impact parameter is zero, actually realises the distance of closest approach. (ii) CALCULATION. At the distance of closest approach \(r_0\) the whole kinetic energy has become potential energy, so \(E_K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_0}\), giving \(r_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^2}{E_K}\). Here \(Z = 79\) and \(E_K = 3.95\) MeV \(= 3.95 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\) J \(= 6.32 \times 10^{-13}\) J. Substituting, \(r_0 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{3.95 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13}} = \dfrac{3.64 \times 10^{-26}}{6.32 \times 10^{-13}}\). Hence \(r_0 = 5.76 \times 10^{-14}\) m, that is \(57.6 \times 10^{-15}\) m or about 57.6 fm. (This is far larger than the radius of a gold nucleus, about 7 fm, which is why the alpha particle never actually touches the nucleus at this energy.)

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
(i) State three postulates of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom.
(ii) Find the angular momentum of an electron revolving in the second orbit in Bohr's hydrogen atom.
rows.solution: (i) BOHR'S POSTULATES. 1. An electron in an atom can revolve in certain stable orbits WITHOUT emitting radiant energy, contrary to what classical electromagnetism demands of an accelerating charge. These allowed orbits are called the stationary states of the atom. 2. The electron revolves around the nucleus only in those orbits for which its angular momentum is an INTEGRAL MULTIPLE of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\), that is \(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), where \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\) and \(h\) is Planck's constant. This is the quantisation condition that selects the stationary states. 3. When an electron makes a transition from one of these non-radiating orbits to another of LOWER energy, a photon is emitted whose energy equals the difference between the two states, \(h\nu = E_i - E_f\). (Absorption is the reverse process.) (ii) ANGULAR MOMENTUM IN THE SECOND ORBIT. By the second postulate the angular momentum in the \(n\)th orbit is \(L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\). For the SECOND orbit \(n = 2\), so \(L = \dfrac{2h}{2\pi} = \dfrac{h}{\pi} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{3.14}\). Hence \(L = 2.1 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\).

rows.stem:
(i) Explain how free electrons in a metal at constant temperature attain an average velocity under the action of an electric field. Hence obtain an expression for it.
(ii) Consider two conducting wires A and B of the same diameter but made of different materials joined in series across a battery. The number density of electrons in A is 1.5 times that in B. Find the ratio of drift velocity of electrons in wire A to that in wire B.
rows.solution: (i) HOW THE FREE ELECTRONS ATTAIN AN AVERAGE VELOCITY. In a metal at a constant temperature the free electrons are already in rapid random thermal motion, colliding constantly with the ions of the lattice. Because the directions of this motion are completely random, the average velocity of the electrons is zero and there is no net current. When an external electric field \(\vec{E}\) is applied, each electron of charge \(-e\) experiences a force \(\vec{F} = -e\vec{E}\) and so an acceleration \(\vec{a} = -\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}\) BETWEEN collisions. The electron does not accelerate indefinitely, however: after a short free flight it collides with a lattice ion and emerges with a velocity whose direction is once again random, so whatever it gained from the field is wiped out at every collision. The outcome is a small, steady average velocity in the direction opposite to \(\vec{E}\), superposed on the much larger random motion. This average velocity is the DRIFT VELOCITY. EXPRESSION. Let \(\vec{u}_i\) be the thermal velocity of the \(i\)th electron immediately after its last collision and \(t_i\) the time elapsed since that collision. Its velocity now is \(\vec{v}_i = \vec{u}_i - \dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}t_i\). Averaging over all the free electrons, \((\vec{v}_i)_{avg} = (\vec{u}_i)_{avg} - \dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}(t_i)_{avg}\). The post-collision velocities are random in direction, so \((\vec{u}_i)_{avg} = 0\). Writing the average time between collisions -- the relaxation time -- as \(\tau\), the drift velocity is \(\vec{v}_d = -\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}\tau\), of magnitude \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\). This is a constant velocity, directed opposite to the field, and it is fixed once the temperature (and hence \(\tau\)) is fixed. (ii) RATIO OF THE DRIFT VELOCITIES. The current in a wire of cross-sectional area \(A\) carrying free-electron number density \(n\) is \(I = neAv_d\), so \(v_d = \dfrac{I}{neA}\). The wires A and B are joined in SERIES, so exactly the same current \(I\) passes through both, and they have the same diameter, so \(A\) is the same for both. Every quantity except \(n\) is therefore common, and \(v_d \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\). Given \(n_A = 1.5\,n_B\), \(\dfrac{v_{dA}}{v_{dB}} = \dfrac{n_B}{n_A} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). The drift velocity in wire A is thus two-thirds of that in wire B: the wire with more carriers needs each of them to move more slowly to pass the same current.

rows.stem:
(i) A cell emf of (E) and internal resistance (r) is connected across a variable load resistance (R). Draw plots showing the variation of terminal voltage V with (i) R and (ii) the current (I) in the load.
(ii) Three cells, each of emf E but internal resistances 2r, 3r and 6r are connected in parallel across a resistor R.
Obtain expressions for (i) current flowing in the circuit, and (ii) the terminal potential difference across the equivalent cell.
rows.solution: (i) THE TWO PLOTS. For a cell of emf \(E\) and internal resistance \(r\) driving a load \(R\), the current is \(I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}\) and the terminal voltage is \(V = E - Ir = \dfrac{ER}{R + r}\). VARIATION OF V WITH R: at \(R = 0\), a short circuit, \(V = 0\); as \(R\) increases \(V\) rises, steeply at first and then more and more gently, approaching the horizontal line \(V = E\) asymptotically as \(R \rightarrow \infty\). So the curve starts at the origin and saturates at \(E\), which is never quite reached while any current flows. VARIATION OF V WITH I: writing the relation as \(V = E - Ir\) shows \(V\) to be a straight line in \(I\), with intercept \(E\) on the \(V\)-axis and constant negative slope \(-r\). It falls steadily and meets the \(I\)-axis at the short-circuit current \(I = \dfrac{E}{r}\). The magnitude of the slope of this line is the internal resistance of the cell. (ii) THREE CELLS IN PARALLEL. The three cells have equal emf \(E\) and internal resistances \(2r\), \(3r\) and \(6r\), and are connected in parallel across \(R\). For cells in parallel the equivalent internal resistance is given by \(\dfrac{1}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2} + \dfrac{1}{r_3} = \dfrac{1}{2r} + \dfrac{1}{3r} + \dfrac{1}{6r} = \dfrac{3 + 2 + 1}{6r} = \dfrac{1}{r}\), so \(r_{eq} = r\). The equivalent emf follows from \(\dfrac{E_{eq}}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{E_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{E_2}{r_2} + \dfrac{E_3}{r_3} = \dfrac{E}{2r} + \dfrac{E}{3r} + \dfrac{E}{6r} = \dfrac{E}{r}\), which with \(r_{eq} = r\) gives \(E_{eq} = E\). This is what should be expected: cells of equal emf connected in parallel cannot raise the emf, they only lower the internal resistance and so allow a larger current to be drawn. CURRENT FLOWING IN THE CIRCUIT: \(I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{R + r_{eq}} = \dfrac{E}{R + r}\). TERMINAL POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE ACROSS THE EQUIVALENT CELL: \(V = E_{eq} - I r_{eq} = E - \dfrac{E}{R + r}\times r = \dfrac{E(R + r) - Er}{R + r}\), so \(V = \dfrac{ER}{R + r}\), which is of course also \(IR\), the potential difference across the external resistor.

rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Draw the circuit arrangement for studying V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode in (i) forward biasing and (ii) reverse biasing. Draw the typical V-I characteristics of a silicon diode. Describe briefly the following terms : (i) minority carrier injection in forward biasing and (ii) breakdown voltage in reverse biasing.
rows.solution: CIRCUIT FOR FORWARD BIAS. Connect the p-side of the diode to the POSITIVE terminal of a variable dc supply and the n-side to the negative terminal, through a key. Connect a VOLTMETER across the diode to read the voltage across it, and a MILLIAMMETER in series with it, because the forward current is of the order of milliamperes. CIRCUIT FOR REVERSE BIAS. Reverse the battery, so that the p-side goes to the NEGATIVE terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal. Keep the voltmeter across the diode, but replace the milliammeter by a MICROAMMETER, because the reverse current is only a few microamperes. TYPICAL V-I CHARACTERISTIC OF A SILICON DIODE. Plot forward voltage to the right along the \(V\)-axis with forward current in mA upwards, and reverse voltage to the left with reverse current in \(\mu\mathrm{A}\) downwards -- note that the two halves are drawn to very different current scales. In forward bias the current is negligible until the voltage reaches the threshold or knee voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon, after which it rises extremely steeply and almost vertically. In reverse bias only a tiny, almost constant reverse saturation current of a few \(\mu\mathrm{A}\) flows, until the breakdown voltage \(V_{br}\) is reached, where the reverse current increases sharply. MINORITY CARRIER INJECTION IN FORWARD BIAS. Forward bias opposes the built-in barrier potential, so the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls, allowing the majority carriers to cross the junction: electrons from the n-side cross into the p-side, and holes from the p-side cross into the n-side. Once across, each of them is a MINORITY carrier in the region it has entered, so the concentration of minority carriers just beyond the junction is raised far above its equilibrium value. This process is called minority carrier injection, and the diffusion of these injected carriers away from the junction is what constitutes the forward current. BREAKDOWN VOLTAGE IN REVERSE BIAS. Under reverse bias the depletion region widens, the barrier rises and only the small reverse saturation current flows. If the reverse voltage is raised to a certain critical value, the electric field in the depletion layer becomes strong enough either to break covalent bonds directly (Zener breakdown) or to give the few free carriers enough energy to ionise atoms by collision, multiplying the carriers rapidly (avalanche breakdown). At that voltage the reverse current increases abruptly and sharply while the voltage across the diode stays almost constant. This critical reverse voltage is the BREAKDOWN VOLTAGE. An ordinary junction diode is destroyed if operated there, whereas a Zener diode is specially designed to work at it and is used for voltage regulation.
