rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: Name two important processes involved in the formation of a p-n junction diode. With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of junction diode as a full wave rectifier. Draw its input and output waveforms. State the characteristic property of a junction diode that makes it suitable for rectification.
rows.solution: TWO IMPORTANT PROCESSES IN THE FORMATION OF A p-n JUNCTION: DIFFUSION and DRIFT. When the p- and n-regions are formed, the large concentration gradient makes holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side; this is DIFFUSION. The immobile ionised acceptor and donor ions left behind create a depletion region carrying a built-in electric field directed from n to p, and this field sweeps minority carriers across the junction in the opposite sense; this is DRIFT. The junction settles into equilibrium when the drift current exactly balances the diffusion current, leaving a barrier potential across the depletion region. FULL WAVE RECTIFIER -- CIRCUIT. The ac input is applied to the primary of a CENTRE-TAP TRANSFORMER. The two ends of the secondary, A and B, are connected to the p-sides of two diodes \(\mathrm{D}_1\) and \(\mathrm{D}_2\); the n-sides of the two diodes are joined together and taken to one end of the load resistor \(\mathrm{R}_L\), whose other end is returned to the CENTRE TAP of the secondary. The rectified output is taken across \(\mathrm{R}_L\). WORKING. Since the two halves of the secondary lie on opposite sides of the centre tap, the voltages at A and B are always out of phase with each other. When the voltage at A is positive with respect to the centre tap, \(\mathrm{D}_1\) is forward biased and conducts, while \(\mathrm{D}_2\), being reverse biased, does not; a current passes through \(\mathrm{R}_L\). In the next half cycle A becomes negative and B positive, so \(\mathrm{D}_2\) conducts and \(\mathrm{D}_1\) does not. The essential point is that in BOTH half cycles the current through the load flows in the SAME direction, so both halves of the input are used and the output is unidirectional -- this is why it is called a full wave rectifier. INPUT AND OUTPUT WAVEFORMS. The input at A is a full sine wave and the input at B is the same sine wave inverted. The output across \(\mathrm{R}_L\) is a train of positive humps with no gaps between them, one hump from each half cycle of the input, so the output ripple frequency is TWICE the input frequency; alternate humps are contributed by \(\mathrm{D}_1\) and \(\mathrm{D}_2\). CHARACTERISTIC PROPERTY THAT MAKES IT SUITABLE. A junction diode conducts appreciably only when it is FORWARD biased and offers a very high resistance when reverse biased -- it allows current to pass in one direction only. This one-way conduction is exactly what is needed to convert an alternating current into a direct one.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram to show the working of a compound microscope. Obtain the expression for the total magnification for the final image to be formed at the near point.
(ii) In a compound microscope an object is placed at a distance of 1.5 cm from the objective of focal length 1.25 cm. If the eye-piece has a focal length of 5 cm and the final image is formed at the near point, find the magnifying power of the microscope.
rows.solution: (i) RAY DIAGRAM AND TOTAL MAGNIFICATION. Draw two converging lenses on a common axis: the OBJECTIVE O, of small focal length \(f_0\) and small aperture, and the EYEPIECE E, of somewhat larger focal length \(f_e\). Place the object \(AB\) just beyond the first focus of the objective, so that the objective forms a real, inverted and magnified image \(A'B'\) on the other side. This image is arranged to fall just INSIDE the focal length of the eyepiece, which then acts as a simple microscope and forms the final image \(A''B''\) -- virtual, still inverted with respect to the object, and greatly magnified -- at the near point, a distance \(D = 25\) cm from the eye. Mark the direction of propagation of light on the rays. The linear magnification produced by the objective is \(m_0 = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{L}{f_0}\), where \(h\) and \(h'\) are the heights of the object and of the intermediate image, and \(L\) is the tube length, the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece. The eyepiece, used with the final image at the near point, gives the angular magnification \(m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\). The total magnification is the product of the two, \(m = m_0 \times m_e = \dfrac{L}{f_0}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)\). (Written in terms of the actual image and object distances at the objective this is \(m = \dfrac{v_0}{u_0}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)\), which is the form used in the calculation below.) (ii) CALCULATION. Given \(u_0 = -1.5\) cm, \(f_0 = 1.25\) cm, \(f_e = 5\) cm and \(D = 25\) cm. For the objective, \(\dfrac{1}{f_0} = \dfrac{1}{v_0} - \dfrac{1}{u_0}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{v_0} = \dfrac{1}{1.25} - \dfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.8 - 0.6667 = \dfrac{2}{15}\), giving \(v_0 = \dfrac{15}{2} = 7.5\) cm. Hence \(|m_0| = \left|\dfrac{v_0}{u_0}\right| = \dfrac{7.5}{1.5} = 5\). For the eyepiece with the final image at the near point, \(|m_e| = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e} = 1 + \dfrac{25}{5} = 6\). The magnifying power of the microscope is therefore \(m = |m_0| \times |m_e| = 5 \times 6 = 30\).

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram for the formation of image of an object by an astronomical telescope, in normal adjustment. Obtain the expression for its magnifying power.
(ii) The magnifying power of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment is 2.9 and the objective and the eyepiece are separated by a distance of 150 cm. Find the focal lengths of the two lenses.
rows.solution: (i) RAY DIAGRAM AND MAGNIFYING POWER. Draw the OBJECTIVE, a converging lens of large aperture and long focal length \(f_0\), and the EYEPIECE, a converging lens of short focal length \(f_e\), on a common axis and separated by \(f_0 + f_e\). Rays from a distant object arrive effectively parallel, making an angle \(\alpha\) with the axis, and the objective brings them to a real, inverted image \(A'B'\) in its focal plane. In NORMAL ADJUSTMENT the two lenses are so placed that this intermediate image lies exactly at the FIRST FOCUS of the eyepiece; the eyepiece therefore sends out a parallel beam and the final image is formed at INFINITY, subtending an angle \(\beta\) at the eye. The final image is inverted with respect to the object, which does not matter for astronomical work. The magnifying power is defined as the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle subtended by the object at the unaided eye, \(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\). If \(h\) is the height of the intermediate image \(A'B'\), then for small angles \(\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_0}\) and \(\beta = \dfrac{h}{f_e}\), so \(m = \dfrac{h/f_e}{h/f_0} = \dfrac{f_0}{f_e}\). A large magnifying power thus needs an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length, and in normal adjustment the length of the telescope tube is \(L = f_0 + f_e\). (ii) CALCULATION. Given \(m = 2.9\) and the separation \(f_0 + f_e = 150\) cm. From \(m = \dfrac{f_0}{f_e} = 2.9 = \dfrac{29}{10}\) we have \(f_0 = 2.9 f_e\). Substituting into the separation, \(2.9 f_e + f_e = 150\), so \(3.9 f_e = 150\) and \(f_e = \dfrac{150}{3.9} = 38.5\) cm to one decimal place. Then \(f_0 = 150 - 38.5 = 111.5\) cm. So the objective has a focal length of about 111.5 cm and the eyepiece about 38.5 cm; a quick check confirms \(\dfrac{111.5}{38.5} \approx 2.9\).

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: An object AB is kept in front of a composite convex lens, as shown in figure. Will the lens produce one image ? If not, explain.
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Considering image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, lens maker's formula is obtained. It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. This formula helps us obtain a relation between u, v and f for a lens. Lenses form images of objects and they are used in a number of optical devices, for example microscopes and telescopes.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'as shown in figure' and the whole question is what the drawing shows about the lens's construction. Described here: an upright object drawn as a vertical arrow whose head is labelled A and whose foot, labelled B, sits on a horizontal dashed principal axis; to the right of it a biconvex lens drawn symmetrically about that axis, the axis running through it. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the two region labels printed inside the lens body and what they denote — they are exactly the composite structure the question asks the student to notice, and naming them would state the answer. Page idx 20.
rows.solution: NO -- the lens will produce TWO images. The figure shows the convex lens divided along the principal axis into an upper half made of material of refractive index \(n_1\) and a lower half made of material of refractive index \(n_2\), the two being different. By the lens maker's formula \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\), the focal length of a lens depends on the refractive index of its material, so the upper and lower halves have DIFFERENT focal lengths. Rays from the object \(AB\) that pass through the upper half converge at one point, and those that pass through the lower half converge at a different point, each half forming its own complete image of the object. Hence two images are produced, at two different positions along the axis.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A real image of an object formed by a convex lens is observed on a screen. If the screen is removed, will the image still be formed ? Explain.
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Considering image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, lens maker's formula is obtained. It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. This formula helps us obtain a relation between u, v and f for a lens. Lenses form images of objects and they are used in a number of optical devices, for example microscopes and telescopes.
rows.solution: YES -- the image is still formed. A real image exists at the place where the refracted rays actually intersect, and that position is fixed entirely by the object distance and the focal length of the lens; the screen plays no part in creating it. What the screen does is make the image VISIBLE, by diffusely scattering the light falling on it so that it can be seen from many directions at once. If the screen is removed, the rays still converge to the same point and the image is still there; it simply cannot be seen on a surface any more. It can still be observed by placing the eye beyond that point, so as to receive the rays after they have crossed and begun to diverge again, or by putting another screen back at the same place.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A double convex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.55 with both faces of the same radius of curvature. Find the radius of curvature required if focal length is 20 cm.
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Considering image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, lens maker's formula is obtained. It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. This formula helps us obtain a relation between u, v and f for a lens. Lenses form images of objects and they are used in a number of optical devices, for example microscopes and telescopes.
rows.solution: For a thin lens the lens maker's formula is \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\), where \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are the radii of curvature of the first and second surfaces, taken with the usual sign convention. For a DOUBLE CONVEX lens with both faces of the same radius of curvature \(R\), the first surface bulges towards the incoming light and the second away from it, so \(R_1 = +R\) and \(R_2 = -R\). Substituting, \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} + \dfrac{1}{R}\right) = (n - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\), which rearranges to \(R = 2(n - 1)f\). With \(n = 1.55\) and \(f = 20\) cm, \(R = 2(1.55 - 1)(20) = 2 \times 0.55 \times 20 = 22\) cm. Each face must therefore have a radius of curvature of 22 cm.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: Two convex lenses A and B of focal lengths 15 cm and 10 cm respectively are placed coaxially 'd' distance apart. A point object is kept at a distance of 30 cm in front of lens A. Find the value of 'd' so that the rays emerging from lens B are parallel to its principal axis.
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Considering image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, lens maker's formula is obtained. It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. This formula helps us obtain a relation between u, v and f for a lens. Lenses form images of objects and they are used in a number of optical devices, for example microscopes and telescopes.
rows.solution: Treat the two lenses one after the other, the image formed by A acting as the object for B. FOR LENS A: \(f = 15\) cm and \(u = -30\) cm. Using \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\), \(\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{(-30)} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{1}{30}\), so \(v_1 = 30\) cm. Lens A therefore forms a real image 30 cm to its right. (This is the familiar result that an object placed at \(2f\) gives an image at \(2f\) on the other side.) FOR LENS B: the rays emerging from B are required to be parallel to the principal axis, which means the final image is formed at INFINITY. A lens sends out a parallel beam only when the object for it lies exactly at its FIRST FOCUS. So the image formed by lens A must fall at the focus of lens B, a distance \(f_B = 10\) cm in front of B. The separation between the lenses is therefore \(d = v_1 + f_B = 30 + 10 = 40\) cm.

rows.stem: Find the equivalent capacitance between points A and B in the given diagram.
rows.context: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. The two conductors have equal and opposite charges with a potential difference between them. The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the geometrical configuration (shape, size and separation) of the system and also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They are used to store charges. Like resistors, capacitors can be arranged in series or parallel or a combination of both to obtain desired value of capacitance.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'in the given diagram' and gives no circuit at all, so the drawing is the entire question. Described here: a capacitor network drawn between a terminal marked A on the left and a terminal marked B on the right, containing SIX capacitors, every one of them labelled C. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the topology — which capacitors lie in which branch and which nodes they join — since that is what the equivalent capacitance is computed from. Page idx 22.
rows.solution: Name the junctions along the horizontal line from A to B as \(A\), \(M\), \(N\), \(B\) in order. The six capacitors, each of capacitance \(C\), then join \(A\)-\(M\), \(M\)-\(N\) and \(N\)-\(B\) along that line, \(A\)-\(N\) along the upper branch, \(M\)-\(B\) along the middle-lower branch, and \(A\)-\(B\) directly along the bottom branch. The first five of these form a WHEATSTONE BRIDGE, with \(M\)-\(N\) as the bridge arm. It is BALANCED, because the ratio of the capacitances in the two arms is the same on each side, \(\dfrac{C_{AM}}{C_{MB}} = \dfrac{C_{AN}}{C_{NB}} = 1\). Junctions \(M\) and \(N\) are therefore at the same potential, the bridge capacitor between them carries no charge, and it may be removed without changing anything. What is left of the bridge is two paths, \(A \rightarrow M \rightarrow B\) and \(A \rightarrow N \rightarrow B\), each consisting of two capacitors in SERIES and so worth \(\dfrac{C \times C}{C + C} = \dfrac{C}{2}\), and these two paths are in PARALLEL, giving \(\dfrac{C}{2} + \dfrac{C}{2} = C\). Finally this combination is in parallel with the capacitor joining A straight to B along the bottom branch, so the equivalent capacitance is \(C_{net} = C + C = 2C\).

rows.stem: A dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor. The electric field between the plates decreases. Explain.
rows.context: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. The two conductors have equal and opposite charges with a potential difference between them. The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the geometrical configuration (shape, size and separation) of the system and also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They are used to store charges. Like resistors, capacitors can be arranged in series or parallel or a combination of both to obtain desired value of capacitance.
rows.solution: A dielectric is made up of molecules which are, or which become in a field, tiny electric dipoles. When the slab is placed between the charged plates, the field \(E_0\) of the plates aligns these dipoles along itself. Inside the slab the positive end of each dipole sits against the negative end of the next, so their charges cancel everywhere except at the two faces, leaving a layer of NEGATIVE bound charge on the face next to the positive plate and a layer of POSITIVE bound charge on the face next to the negative plate. These polarisation charges set up their own field \(E_p\) inside the slab, and because of the way they are arranged this field is directed OPPOSITE to the applied field. The net field inside is therefore the difference of the two, \(E = E_0 - E_p\), which is necessarily smaller than \(E_0\). Quantitatively \(E = \dfrac{E_0}{K}\), where \(K\) is the dielectric constant of the material, and since \(K > 1\) for every dielectric the field between the plates is reduced. (This reduction of the field, at constant charge, lowers the potential difference and so raises the capacitance to \(KC_0\).)

rows.stem: A capacitor A of capacitance C, having charge Q is connected across another uncharged capacitor B of capacitance 2C. Find an expression for (a) the potential difference across the combination and (b) the charge lost by capacitor A.
rows.context: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. The two conductors have equal and opposite charges with a potential difference between them. The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the geometrical configuration (shape, size and separation) of the system and also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They are used to store charges. Like resistors, capacitors can be arranged in series or parallel or a combination of both to obtain desired value of capacitance.
rows.solution: Capacitor A, of capacitance \(C\), carries charge \(Q\), so its initial potential difference is \(V = \dfrac{Q}{C}\). It is then connected across the uncharged capacitor B of capacitance \(2C\). The two are joined plate to plate, so they end up in PARALLEL and must settle to a common final potential difference \(V'\); charge flows from A to B until this happens. (a) POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE ACROSS THE COMBINATION. Charge is conserved during the sharing, and the capacitance of the parallel combination is \(C_{eq} = C + 2C = 3C\). Hence \(V' = \dfrac{Q_{total}}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{Q}{3C}\), which is also \(\dfrac{V}{3}\), i.e. one third of the original potential difference. (b) CHARGE LOST BY CAPACITOR A. After the connection the charge remaining on A is \(Q_A' = C V' = C \times \dfrac{Q}{3C} = \dfrac{Q}{3}\), whereas it began with \(Q_A = CV = Q\). The charge lost by capacitor A is therefore \(\Delta Q = Q - \dfrac{Q}{3} = \dfrac{2Q}{3}\). That charge is not destroyed: it is exactly the charge \(2C \times \dfrac{Q}{3C} = \dfrac{2Q}{3}\) which has flowed onto capacitor B. (Some ENERGY is lost, however, as heat in the connecting wires, since the stored energy falls from \(\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\) to \(\dfrac{Q^2}{6C}\).)

rows.stem: Two slabs of dielectric constants 2K and K fill the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and plate separation d as shown in figure. Find an expression for capacitance of the system.
rows.context: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. The two conductors have equal and opposite charges with a potential difference between them. The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the geometrical configuration (shape, size and separation) of the system and also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They are used to store charges. Like resistors, capacitors can be arranged in series or parallel or a combination of both to obtain desired value of capacitance.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem gives the plate area A, the separation d and the two dielectric constants, but NOT how the two slabs divide the space, and that division is printed only in the drawing. Described here: a rectangle representing the gap between the plates, split by a vertical line into a left region hatched with diagonal lines and labelled 2K and a right region hatched with horizontal lines and labelled K; a dimension line beneath the whole rectangle is labelled d, and two dimension lines above it label the widths of the two regions. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the two width labels themselves — they are the only thing fixing how the slabs share the separation and the expression cannot be written without them. Page idx 22.
rows.solution: Read the arrangement off the figure: the two slabs fill the gap one BEHIND the other along the direction of the field, the slab of dielectric constant \(2K\) occupying a thickness \(\dfrac{d}{3}\) and the slab of dielectric constant \(K\) occupying the remaining \(\dfrac{2d}{3}\), each spanning the full plate area \(A\). Slabs stacked this way behave as two capacitors in SERIES, because the same charge is induced on each interface while the potential differences across the two portions add up to the total. Treating each portion as a parallel plate capacitor of area \(A\) and its own thickness, \(C_1 = \dfrac{(2K)\varepsilon_0 A}{d/3} = \dfrac{6K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\) and \(C_2 = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{2d/3} = \dfrac{3K\varepsilon_0 A}{2d}\). For capacitors in series, \(\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} = \dfrac{d}{6K\varepsilon_0 A} + \dfrac{2d}{3K\varepsilon_0 A} = \dfrac{d + 4d}{6K\varepsilon_0 A} = \dfrac{5d}{6K\varepsilon_0 A}\). Hence the capacitance of the system is \(C_{eq} = \dfrac{6K\varepsilon_0 A}{5d}\). (As a check, this is \(\dfrac{6K}{5}\) times the capacitance \(\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\) of the empty capacitor, so the dielectrics raise the capacitance, as they must.)
